lines.text: In twenty twelve, one company lost four hundred sixty million dollars in forty-five minutes.
In twenty twenty, a bank accidentally sent out nearly nine hundred million dollars.
And one man gave up a piece of Apple for just eight hundred dollars.
Some of these mistakes nearly destroyed a company. Others became famous lessons that banks and engineers still learn from today.
These are some of the most expensive mistakes in history.
Some were typos. Some were software bugs. And one was simply a bad decision.
We'll count them down, from number seven to number one. And number one is so big, it barely feels real.
Number seven. In nineteen ninety-nine, NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter had flown four hundred sixteen million miles to reach Mars.
On September twenty-third, it was supposed to swing into orbit. Instead, it flew far too close to the planet, and was never heard from again.
The reason? Lockheed Martin, which built the spacecraft, sent its thruster data in pounds of force. NASA's navigation team assumed the numbers were in newtons.
One pound of force is about four and a half newtons. So every correction was off by more than four times, and nobody noticed.
And because the numbers didn't look obviously wrong, the error kept growing quietly, mile after mile.
A hundred and twenty-five million dollar spacecraft, lost because two teams used different units.
Lesson one: the most dangerous errors are the ones that look completely normal.

els.small: The worst errors look completely normal

lines.text: But at least that one was in space. Number six happened with a single keyboard.
Number six. Tokyo, December eighth, two thousand five.
A trader at Mizuho Securities wanted to sell one share of a new company called J-Com, for six hundred ten thousand yen.
Instead, the numbers got swapped. The order said: sell six hundred ten thousand shares, for one yen each.
In finance, this is called a fat-finger error. Someone hits the wrong key, or types the right numbers into the wrong box.
And J-Com didn't even have that many shares. The order was forty-one times bigger than all the shares that existed.
Mizuho tried to cancel it right away, but a glitch at the Tokyo Stock Exchange kept the cancel from going through.
The damage: about forty billion yen, more than three hundred million dollars, from one swapped number.
Years later, a court said the exchange was mostly to blame, and ordered it to pay around a hundred and twenty million dollars. It still left a huge hole.
Since then, trading systems have added more automatic checks to block orders that are clearly impossible. But as number five shows, software can fail in other ways.
Number five. August first, twenty twelve. Knight Capital was one of the biggest stock traders in America.
That morning, it installed new trading software on its eight servers. But on one of them, the update never arrived.
Before the market opened, the system sent ninety-seven warning emails. Nobody acted on them.
At nine thirty, the market opened, and that one server woke up old code that hadn't been used in years.
In forty-five minutes, it fired off more than four million orders.
By the time it was stopped, Knight had lost four hundred sixty million dollars.
That's more than ten million dollars, every single minute.
Its stock crashed more than seventy percent, and days later it needed a four hundred million dollar rescue just to survive.
A year later, Knight was taken over by a rival, and the company disappeared as an independent firm.
Number four. A city called Newport, in Wales.

spec.chapsub: THE HARD DRIVE IN THE TRASH

lines.text: In the early days of bitcoin, a computer engineer named James Howells collected around eight thousand bitcoin, back when they were worth almost nothing.
In twenty thirteen, an old hard drive holding the keys to those coins was thrown out with the trash, and it ended up in the local landfill.
Today, those eight thousand bitcoin would be worth more than six hundred million dollars.
And the drive isn't sitting on top. He believes it's buried somewhere in an area holding around a hundred thousand tonnes of waste.
For over ten years, he tried to get permission to dig. He offered the city a share of the money. He even talked about buying the whole landfill.
But in twenty twenty-five, the courts said no. And the city plans to close the site for good.
Still, at least that money was never really in someone else's hands. Number three is about a bank that sent away almost a billion dollars by accident.
Number three. New York, August eleventh, twenty twenty.
Citibank was supposed to send a routine interest payment for the cosmetics company Revlon. About seven point eight million dollars.
Instead, after a mix-up in how the payment was entered, it paid back Revlon's entire loan. Nearly nine hundred million dollars, years before it was due.
That's more than a hundred times bigger than the payment it was supposed to make.
Some lenders sent the money back. But others kept about five hundred million dollars, and basically said: thanks, that's ours now.
And in twenty twenty-one, a judge actually agreed with them.
Citibank appealed. In twenty twenty-two, a higher court reversed the ruling, and said Citi had the right to get its money back.
Two years of court fights, all because of a few clicks. It became a famous lesson about how payment screens and approvals are designed.
Number two. Seoul, South Korea, April twenty eighteen.
Samsung Securities wanted to pay its employees a dividend of one thousand won per share. That's less than one dollar.
But an employee entered one thousand shares, instead of one thousand won.
In seconds, about two point eight billion new shares appeared out of thin air. More than thirty times all the shares that really existed.
On paper, they were worth around a hundred and five billion dollars.
These were ghost shares. But sixteen employees sold about five million of them anyway, worth around a hundred and eighty-seven million dollars.
The company's CEO later resigned.
South Korea's regulators stepped in, and even years later, courts were still ordering Samsung Securities to pay compensation to investors.
A hundred and five billion dollars on paper is huge. But the number one mistake on this list wasn't a typo at all.
And number one. California, nineteen seventy-six.
Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak were starting a new computer company called Apple. They brought in a third partner, Ronald Wayne, and gave him ten percent.
Back then, Apple was just a tiny startup, and nobody knew if it would survive.
But just twelve days later, Wayne gave up his share. For eight hundred dollars.
Why? He later said he felt like he was standing in the shadow of giants.
Later, he took another fifteen hundred dollars to drop any claim to the company.
Today, Apple is worth around four trillion dollars.
Even after all the new shares Apple created over the years, his ten percent could be worth somewhere between seventy-five and three hundred sixty billion dollars.
And the wildest part? He says he has no regrets.
So what do all these mistakes have in common? Most of them weren't made by stupid people.

els.txt: What do they have in common?

lines.text: They were made by smart people, in a hurry, trusting a number they never double-checked.
A unit nobody converted. A number typed the wrong way round. Ninety-seven emails nobody read.
So next time you send money, sign something, or hit confirm, take five extra seconds. It might be the cheapest insurance you'll ever get.
Because as you just saw, the biggest losses rarely come from one huge decision. They come from tiny moments that nobody took seriously.
Which of these mistakes shocked you the most? Tell me in the comments. And if you want more stories like this, subscribe.
